nameStory: The garden tulip gets its name from the Persian word 'dulband' meaning turban, referring to the flower's distinctive cup shape that resembles a wrapped turban. The species name 'gesneriana' honors Conrad Gesner, a 16th-century Swiss naturalist who first described these showy spring beauties in European botanical literature.
description: Garden tulips are the classic spring bulb flowers we all know and love, with their iconic cup-shaped blooms perched atop straight stems. These plants typically grow 12-24 inches tall with a single large flower crowning each stem. The blooms come in nearly every color except true blue, sitting above several broad, blue-green leaves that emerge directly from the ground. Most garden tulips are actually complex hybrids that have been cultivated for centuries.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six broad, smooth petals form a perfect cup shape, often with a darker center or contrasting edges. The petals feel waxy and substantial to the touch, not papery like some spring flowers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two to six broad, lance-shaped leaves emerge directly from the ground in a rosette pattern. The leaves feel thick and waxy with a blue-green color and smooth edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single sturdy stem rises straight up from the center of the leaf cluster, typically 12-24 inches tall with one flower per stem. The whole plant has a very orderly, symmetrical appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After blooming, develops a three-chambered capsule that splits open to reveal flat, papery seeds. The seed pod has six distinct ridges running lengthwise.

habitat: Garden tulips are almost exclusively found in cultivated settings like gardens, parks, and landscaped areas throughout New England. They prefer well-drained soil and full to partial sun exposure. Occasionally, they may naturalize and persist in abandoned garden sites or spread to nearby areas, but they rarely establish in truly wild habitats.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming season from April through May, with flowers lasting 1-2 weeks. The distinctive cup-shaped blooms and emerging blue-green leaves make identification easiest during this time.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain green for several weeks after flowering, then gradually yellow and die back completely. By mid-summer, the plant has disappeared above ground, returning all energy to the underground bulb.
seasonality.fall: No visible above-ground parts present. This is when gardeners typically plant new bulbs, which need cold winter temperatures to bloom the following spring.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no visible growth above ground. The bulb rests underground, developing next year's flower bud during the cold months.

funFact: Garden tulips are actually one big beautiful lie - most 'species' are complex hybrids of multiple original tulip species that have been bred for so long that their true genetic ancestry is nearly impossible to untangle, making them more of a 'neo-species' than a natural one!
confusionNotes: Early spring tulip shoots can be confused with daffodil shoots, but tulip leaves are broader and flatter while daffodil leaves are narrower and more strap-like. Remember: tulip leaves look like they could wrap around your finger, daffodil leaves are too thin and stiff.
contextualKnowledge: What most people call 'tulips' in their gardens are actually this single hybridized species rather than the many distinct wild tulip species found in Central Asia. The famous Dutch tulip industry is built almost entirely on varieties of this one adaptable garden tulip.
compareHints: Garden tulips are much larger and showier than their wild cousin, the Wild Tulip, which has smaller yellow flowers and a more delicate appearance. Garden tulips also have broader leaves and sturdier stems, while Wild Tulips tend to be more petite overall and are extremely rare in New England. The garden variety's flowers come in many colors while Wild Tulips are typically yellow.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild Tulip differs from common Garden Tulip by being much smaller in all parts, consistently yellow rather than available in many colors, and having narrower leaves.
